reason: The void grid is anchored at the box's minimum corner with its cell count rounded up, so turned over its cells sit elsewhere on the part, and a void whose widening is two cells deep (faces 17, 30, 31) passes the throat test in one orientation only. Python's grid is anchored the same way. A grid centred on the box would map onto itself under these motions; a decision that does not rest on the grid's phase would fix it outright.

A groove's walls are its immediate neighbours in s_lo order, which is not symmetric when bands overlap. This shaft has 60 bands, many split or partial (face 1905 spans -109..149.5); unmoved, the floor (face 2074, Ø180, -164.5..-110.5) has a Ø210 band ending at -169.5 below it and face 1905 starting at -109 above. rot_z90 turns the y axis onto -x, the canonical direction flips the axial coordinate, and the band sorted just below the floor becomes one ending 15 mm short of it, so the floor is not joined and no groove is found. Python behaves the same (checked: recognise_grooves on the part rotated 90° about z returns []). Choosing each wall as the band nearest the floor's end, rather than by s_lo order, would make it symmetric, but it does not keep Python's answers: tried (the lower wall the band starting and ending below the floor's start and end whose end is nearest the floor's start, the upper wall likewise above), the corpus run loses this file's unmoved groove, which Python finds, and finds one on cgb243 that Python does not; the captured calls still matched. With overlapping bands Python's own answer depends on the axis direction, so a motion-invariant rule must differ from it on one of the two; the choice is a change to the specification, left to the maintainer.
